justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across time horizons, starting near 45.3 at the one-day mark and rising gradually to 46.2 at one month. This pattern likely reflects a baseline assumption of mean-reverting behavior around a slightly positive trend, where near-term momentum carries forward but gradually gives way to longer-run fundamental anchors. The one-day estimate is essentially anchored to current observed conditions with minimal adjustment, while the one-week and one-month estimates incorporate a small expected drift, perhaps reflecting anticipated policy direction, seasonal patterns, or gradual improvements in underlying conditions that were visible at the time of forecasting.

The confidence interval widths expand substantially as the horizon extends, which is a standard feature of probabilistic forecasting under uncertainty. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 3 units, reflecting that most short-term variation is fairly contained and predictable within a narrow band. By one week, that span grows to about 6 units, capturing the possibility of meaningful new information arriving — economic releases, geopolitical developments, or shifts in market sentiment. At one month, the interval widens to roughly 12.5 units, acknowledging that over that timeframe, a wide variety of structural and event-driven forces could move outcomes materially in either direction. The asymmetry of risks was treated as roughly balanced in this framing, so the intervals are approximately symmetric around the point estimates.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside even these relatively wide intervals. On the downside, an unexpected shock — a sharp deterioration in financial conditions, a policy reversal, or a geopolitical escalation — could drive outcomes well below 40 at the one-month horizon. On the upside, a strongly positive catalyst such as a surprise policy easing, a major positive data release, or a resolution of an ongoing uncertainty could push above 52.5. These tail events are by definition low-probability but not negligible, and the stated intervals, being 90% confidence intervals, explicitly leave 10% probability mass outside those bounds — meaning roughly one-in-ten outcomes would be expected to fall outside the range even under normal conditions.
